\subsection{Malicious Code}
Malicious code—often known as \textit{malware}—is concisely defined by:\\
\textbf{Definition 10.1} Malicious code is code which deliberately attempts to breach the security policy of the computer on which it is executed.

In everyday informal speech, people often call all types of malicious code a "virus". But technically speaking, malware is divided up into several classes:

\begin{itemize}
  \item \textbf{Virus:} Attaches itself to a program or data and transfers malicious code to nonharmful programs by modifying them.
  \item \textbf{Worm:} An independent program which spreads copies of itself through the net without using infected files.
  \item \textbf{Trojan horse:} A piece of software which has an apparent useful effect, but also a not immediately apparent harmful effect.
  \item \textbf{Logic bomb/timebomb:} Has a harmful effect which does not appear until it is triggered by particular conditions or events.
  \item \textbf{Backdoor/trapdoor:} Gives the attacker (possibly privileged) access to a computer without the attacker having to go through the usual procedures for login or authentication.
  \item \textbf{Spyware:} Sends details about the computer's hardware and/or the user's activities to the attacker.
  \item \textbf{Ransomware:} This comes in two flavours: \textit{Cryptographic ransomware} encrypts the entire disk or the contents of selected files, and demands money from the user to get them decrypted again. \textit{Exposure ransomware} steals private or confidential data from the victim and threatens to expose it if a ransom is not paid. Some types of ransomware do both, first stealing some confidential data, then encrypting some or all files, and then threatening to expose the confidential data in order to press the victim to pay the ransom.
  \item \textbf{Rabbit/bacterium:} Reproduces itself continually, in order to use up all the system's resources.
\end{itemize}

\subsection{BCP Resource Requirements}
A significant part of BCP is to make a plan for how many resources are needed to restore normal operation, and how they are to be organised. This plan involves consideration of factors such as:

\begin{itemize}
  \item \textbf{Personnel}: Who is to be involved in the task of recovery?
  \item \textbf{Roles and resposibilities}: Which person is to be in charge of the recovery process? What do the others do? If some of the persons involved are absent, who will if necessary replace them?
  \item \textbf{Localities}: Which localities are to be used, if operations cannot continue in the usual localities?
  \item \textbf{Equipment}: What equipment must be present in order to continue operations?
  \item \textbf{Outsourcing}: Must there be contact to external partners or suppliers, who can deal with some of the organisation's tasks?
\end{itemize}

It is important to remember that a significant incident puts a heavy psychological strain on the people involved. If you see video recordings from sessions where staff are training to handle incidents, it is common to observe a sense of panic as the trainees see the situation getting more and more out of control. The BCP should stress the importance of keeping calm and doing what the person in charge instructs you to do. This is even more important in the case of a full-scale disaster, which we consider next.

\subsection{Disaster Recovery Planning}
A special task within BCP is the planning of reactions to disasters of various types. A disaster is in this context an incident which is so extensive that it leads to operation of the IT system being interrupted for a significantly long period. This area of BCP is generally known as \emph{Disaster Recovery Planning}, or just \emph{DRP}. Since incidents due to cyberattacks differ in many ways from incidents due to natural or man-made disasters of other types, the more specific term \emph{Cyberincident Recovery Planning}, or just \emph{CIRP}, is often used in such cases instead.

One of the central ideas in DRP is to introduce sufficient \emph{redundancy} ${ }^{1}$ into the systems, so it is possible to survive a disastrous failure in some of them by using the others. For example, you could set up a diesel generator which can be started if there is a failure in the electricity supply. Or you might maintain a complete copy of an important database in another location. Or you may need alternative possibilities for communication if the usual network infrastructure has been damaged or taken over by attackers.

It is important to realise that the redundant elements must be sufficiently separated, so they do not all get hit by the same disaster. This means, amongst other things,

\footnotetext{${ }^{1}$ This means extra items of hardware, software or data, which are not needed during normal operations
}
that the alternative locations must not be in the same building complex, the same electricity supply area, or the same area which can be hit by hurricanes, earthquakes or floods. Similarly, after a cyberattack the normal infrastructure of the IT system may be corrupted, exposing data accessible via this infrastructure to the attackers. So the redundant copies of data, which may be needed for recovery after a cyberattack, must be kept within an infrastructure which is isolated from the normal infrastructure until they are needed.

\section{Further Reading}
David A. Wheeler has published a very useful practical guide to what to do in order to develop secure software: ``\emph{Secure Programming HOWTO}''. It is available free of charge as a web publication [97] and is updated at regular intervals.

A general review and evaluation of a long series of tools for evaluating software security was produced in 2009 by the consultancy Booz Allan Hamilton on behalf of the US Navy [12]. An important part of the evaluation was a description of which competencies people should have in order to make use of the different tools. This is a very important aspect of the use of these often very advanced tools, as inexpert users can manage to do more harm than good. As a clever man (probably Grady Booch, a leading software engineer with IBM) once said: ``A Fool with a Tool is still a Fool''.

A number of organisations produce regular reports on trends in malware, software vulnerabilities and the like. Some of these form part of a general report about data breaches observed during the year, such as the previously mentioned ``\emph{2021 Data Breach Investigations Report}'' from Verizon [93]. Others are more specialised. A particular effort goes into analysing software vulnerabilities in web applications, where there are many forms of attack, of which we have only discussed a small number in this chapter. The non-commercial organisation OWASP (Open Web Application Security Project) produces a report covering this area from time to time, in addition to offering testing tools and publishing much other information on web security. The latest version of the report is currently from 2021 [70].

\subsection{Incomplete Mediation}
The impressive term \textit{incomplete mediation} is used to describe situations where there is no proper control of data. This can lead to random or planned faults. Some simple examples:
\begin{itemize}
  \item Impossible dates in the correct format (e.g. yyyyMMMdd):\\
  1900Feb29, 2048Min32\\
  What do you think happens when these dates are looked up in tables in the program?
  \item Modifiable query fields in a URI. These are often used in applications which perform transactions. For example in an application where a customer buys 20 items with catalogue number 555A, which cost $€ 10$ each, to be delivered by rail, and where the transport costs are $€ 5$, the final URI could look like:\\
  \href{https://www.things.com/order/final?custID=101\&}{https://www.things.com/order/final?custID=101\&}\\
  part=555A\&qty=20\&price=10\&send=rail\&total=205\\
  The web site adds the parameters incrementally to the query field in the URI as data about the transaction is received. If there is no running data control, especially for the calculation of the price, the customer can perhaps change the parameters from his browser, so for example the total price of $€ 205$ is altered to € 105.
\end{itemize}

Vulnerabilities which can expose the system to so-called \textit{software injection}, where an attacker gets a program to execute code which violates the security policy, are also based on incomplete mediation. We look more closely at three of the most important forms, namely SQL injection, LDAP injection and HTML-based cross-site scripting, in Sects. 10.3, 10.4 and 10.5.6.1 below respectively.

\subsection{Time-of-check to Time-of-use (TOCTTOU)}
The name of this type of flaw says everything! A delay between checking permission to perform certain operations and actual use of this permission can make it possible to change the operations in the meantime. An example:
\begin{itemize}
  \item A user tries to write 100 characters into the file abc. A description of the operation is stored in a data structure—a so-called \textit{file descriptor}.
  \item The OS checks the user's rights to write to the file.
  \item While the user's rights are being checked, an attacker changes the descriptor, so it instead refers to the file /etc/passwd, which in systems with an operating system in the Unix family contains information about user accounts.
  \item When the OS informs the user's program that it has permission to write in the file, it will therefore be the file /etc/passwd which gets overwritten.
\end{itemize}

That governments can have an interest in uncovering serious crime, come what may, is perhaps not specially surprising. But data collection and datamining is also very widespread in the commercial world. Knowledge of who you are, what you are interested in, what you purchase and so on can be exploited to provide "intelligent" suggestions for what information you should be given next, but also to send you unasked-for advertisements and other messages, which are matched to the individual recipient. You can easily convince yourself of this by using sales-oriented services such as Amazon, search machines such as Google, Bing and Yahoo, or social media such as Facebook or Twitter.

In many cases, this sort of activity is not illegal, as the users themselves give their consent - either explicitly or implicitly - to the collection of information about themselves. But it is a matter for discussion, whether it is ethically defensible. Large collections of information about their customers' interests and preferences - socalled \emph{customer profiles} - are owned by many companies and financial institutions, and for some of these it gives an extra business opportunity, as the information is sold to others without the customers' knowledge. In that way the profiles can migrate further and further away from the enterprise which originally collected them. This uncontrolled spreading increases the risk of \emph{misuse} of the information, for example for \emph{identity theft}. This is one of the reasons that GDPR gives all individuals the right to object to profiling based on their personal data.

\subsection{Tracking}
Another problematic area from an ethical point of view is the collection of information about which web pages a user has visited - a technique known as \emph{tracking}. Just as in the case of datamining in user information, tracking can be motivated by very different considerations, such as:

\begin{itemize}
  \item \textbf{Combating crime:} The authorities can have an interest in knowing whether particular people visit web pages with jihadi propaganda, information about drugs, instructions for making bombs or other similar topics.
  \item Optimisation of the communication network: For a supplier of Internet services, it can be important to know where the traffic is dense and where it comes from.
  \item Optimisation of advertising and sales: For companies which advertise or sell goods via the Internet, it can be useful to know how many - and preferably also who - visit web pages with their advertisements or their e-shop.\\

\subsection{Cybersecurity in medical equipment}
There is a significant trend in the design of modern medical equipment, that it can be controlled and measurements can be read off with the help of wireless communication. This has the obvious advantage that you can avoid cabled connections, which limit both the patient's and the medical personnel's mobility. On the other hand, it introduces the various risks which are associated with wireless technology: the traffic can perhaps be monitored, modified or blocked by unauthorised persons. Especially equipment such as pacemakers and insulin pumps, which perform life-critical functions, require exceptionally good protection against such attacks.

Try to investigate the literature in order to collect as much knowledge as you can on this topic, with the aim of deciding whether it is a practical or just a theoretical problem. A good starting point would be to try to find mentions of actual attack attempts on medical equipment, and which vulnerabilities in the equipment may have made it possible for the attacks to succeed.

\section{Fermat's Factorisation Algorithm}
\textbf{Step 1:} Take as the first estimate of $a$ the smallest integer larger than or equal to the square root of $n$.\\
\textbf{Step 2:} Check whether $a^{2}-n$ is the square of an integer. If it is, proceed to Step 3 with $b=\sqrt{a^{2}-n}$. If it is not, increase $a$ by 1 and repeat Step 2.\\
\textbf{Step 3:} The algorithm terminates. The factors are the final values of $(a+b)$ and $(a-b)$.

The factors are $(a+b)=4283$ and $(a-b)=3923$, so:

$$
16802209=4283 \times 3923
$$

Fermat's algorithm is efficient, even for large values of $n$, as long as the factors are quite close to the square root of $n$. If they are not, it can take very many iterations of Step 2 before the result is found. For example, while Fermat factorisation of 16802209 only takes 4 iterations of Step 2, factorisation of 219073, whose prime factors are 3001 and 73, takes 1069 iterations, even though it is much smaller than 16802209.

The basic algorithm can be optimised in a number of ways, using various mathematical tricks. For example, a direct way to decide whether $a^{2}-n$ is the square of an integer is to evaluate the square root of $a^{2}-n$ and see whether it in fact is an integer. This is often a time-consuming operation, but if a number $x$ is the square of an integer, then $(x \bmod m)$ for any integer modulus $m$ can only take on certain values. For example, if $m=20$, then $(x \bmod m)$ can only have one of the values $0$, $1,4,5,9$, or $16$. If it has any other value, then $x$ is definitely not a squared integer. This makes it possible to eliminate 14/20 (70\%) of the possible candidates without having to evaluate their square roots at all. More complex optimisations lead to even faster algorithms, such as the Quadratic Sieve and Number Field Sieve, currently the fastest algorithms for finding the prime factors of large integers such as the RSA numbers discussed in Chap. 4.

\subsection{Worm attacks}
It is characteristic of a worm that it itself moves copies of itself from one system to one or more others, where it tries to install itself and if possible send even more copies of itself to new systems. The typical worm is therefore composed of three parts:

\textbf{Searcher:} $\quad$ Code to find potential victims which can be infected;\\
\textbf{Propagator:} Code to transfer the worm to the victim systems;\\
\textbf{Payload:} $\quad$ Code which is to be executed in the victim systems.\\
Some worms are designed to select potential victims at random, while others use information which they find in the local computer to direct their search. Worms which are spread via e-mail will, for example, typically look in personal address books or other files which contain e-mail addresses. Worms which are spread via HTTP will look to see which webservers the local system uses. Other worms use social media as a means of transport, and there it is quite easy to find out who chats with whom. And so on.

When a worm arrives at a new system, it will typically exploit an existing vulnerability there, in order to install and activate itself. Vulnerabilities which can lead to buffer overflow are often used, but worm designers are as a rule very innovative and do not limit themselves to software vulnerabilities-worms sent via e-mail often exploit \textit{social engineering} to persuade the recipient of the mail to click on a link or open an attached document with a malicious content. Note that it is not necessary to find an existing file in which the worm's code can be stored on the victim's system-the worm is an independent unit which works completely autonomously.

In order to hide more effectively, there has been a tendency for worms to use a technique known as \textit{process hollowing}. In rough terms this involves setting up a perfectly normal process, in which a perfectly ordinary program is running, and then to replace the code of that program with the worm's payload. In a typical scenario, the worm will contain a small bootstrap program which starts a perfectly normal process in a suspended state. The operating system will build up the structure of the process and fill it with the code and data sections which belong to the ordinary program. The worm's bootstrap program then replaces one or more of the program's sections with the worm's payload and changes the process' entry point, so execution will start with the malware code. Seen from outside, the process looks like the normal process, with its normal name and so on, but it behaves in a way determined by the malware.

Just like with viruses, the worm's payload can have an almost arbitrary effect on the attacked victim. It can place the system under "remote control", get it to contribute to a DoS attack, overwrite web pages, install a \textit{key logger} to record the user's input (especially access codes, PIN codes, credit card numbers etc.), encrypt the user's files, attack applications which control industrial processes, and many other things. Recovery after some of these attacks can cost society many resources.\\

\subsection{Trapdoor Functions}
Trapdoor functions, which play an important role in modern cryptography, are special types of \textit{one-way functions}. A function $f$ is a one-way function if it is easy to evaluate its value for given argument, for example $x$, whereas it is very difficult to find the value of $x$ if you only know the function value, $f(x)$. A trapdoor function is a oneway function, where there is a hidden secret-the actual \textit{trapdoor}-which can make it easy to find the value of $x$.

A simple example is integer multiplication. The integer 18211891463 is the product of two integers (in fact two prime numbers). Given the two numbers, it is easy to find the product. But if you only know the product, it is relatively hard (at least without the help of a computer) to find its two factors. However, there is a secret which makes it easy: One of the factors is 19391. As soon as you know that, the task is a simple one.

\subsection{Modular Arithmetic}
In cryptography, \textit{modular arithmetic} is often used for constructing trapdoor functions. The modulo operation, mod, is a mathematical operation which calculates the \textit{remainder} of an Euclidean division (also known as an integer division) of two integers. So, for example, $a \bmod n$, gives the remainder after division of the integer $a$ by the integer $n$. Thus:

$$
7 \bmod 5=2, \quad 11 \bmod 5=1, \quad 72 \bmod 3=0
$$

and so on. When you count modulo $n$, you count from 0 up to $n-1$ and then start from 0 again. This way of counting is well known from everyday life: the seconds and the minutes on a clock are counted modulo 60, and the hours are counted modulo 12 or 24. If the time is 51 minutes past the hour, then 20 minutes later the clock will not show that it is $(51+20)$ minutes past, but $(51+20)\bmod 60$, i.e. 11 minutes past.

\textbf{A little warning about notation:} You should notice that there are two alternative notations which are used when discussing modular arithmetic. When we, as above, write $71 \bmod 60=11$, this can be read as "the remainder when 71 is divided by 60 , is equal to 11". But sometimes-especially when the divisor is a large, complicated expression-it is more common to write it in a different way as:

$$
71 \equiv 11 \quad(\bmod 60)
$$

This can be read as "71 and 11 are equivalent when we do arithmetic modulo 60", or, to use a more technical term: "71 is congruent to 11, when we do arithmetic modulo 60". This really says the same, just in a slightly different way. You should notice that two integers are \textit{congruent modulo} $n$, when the difference between them is a multiple of $n$.

Figure 4.18 shows some examples of addition and multiplication performed with modular arithmetic. Addition is easy to understand, especially if you think of the example with the clock. But, if you haven't seen it before, multiplication may seem surprising. For example, when you use multiplication modulo $5,3 \times 2$ is equal to 1. With ordinary arithmetic, the product of two numbers is 1 if one of the numbers is the inverse of the other; for example, $1 / 3$ is the inverse of 3 , often written $3^{-1}$. But if we do multiplication modulo 5 , then 2 must be the inverse of 3 (and vice versa: 3 is the inverse of 2 ). And, as we can see in the figure, 4 must be its own inverse, $4^{-1}$, just like 1 also is its own inverse.\\

\subsection{Passwords}
The use of a userid together with a password is considered to be a simple and reliable way of identifying users. It doesn't need special equipment, and it doesn't give false acceptances or false rejections-either the password is right or else it is wrong. But systems which use passwords can be attacked in various ways. For example, the attacker can:

\begin{itemize}
  \item Try all possible passwords. This is called a \textit{brute-force attack}.
  \item Try many likely passwords taken from a big list or a dictionary. This is called a \textit{dictionary attack}.
  \item Try passwords with (assumed) association to the user, such as dates of family birthdays or anniversaries, names of family members or pets, and so on.
  \item Exploit possibilities for accessing the IT system's internal storage for passwords.
  \item Use techniques of \textit{social engineering} to get the user to reveal the password.
\end{itemize}

\subsection{Password Strength}
A password's \textit{strength} is a measure of how hard it is to find the password by guessing it or using a brute-force attack. If a password is selected by taking $L$ randomly chosen characters from a character set containing $N$ different characters, then there are $N$ raised to the power $L$ possible unique sequences of characters which can be formed. So a brute-force attack will need to try up to $N^{L}$ character sequences in order to be certain to find the right password. This number grows very fast as $N$ and $L$ (the password's length in characters) are increased. Some examples can be seen in Table 9.1. The character set ISO-latin-1 is a commonly used character set which contains all the characters used in Western European languages.

Most smartphones also contain space for an SD card, which works as an \textit{SSD}. The identity module is based on a UICC pilfer-proof smartcard, which contains its own little CPU and memory and has its own little operating system on which a SIM or USIM application runs. The memory is used amongst other things for storing the user's personal information, telephone book and most often also the most recently received text messages. In most smartphones, received text and multimedia messages are transferred to the mobile unit's memory or SD card, as the identity module's memory gets filled up.

If a smartphone is turned on and contains a valid SIM- or USIM-card when it is investigated, it will continue to be able to send and receive text and multimedia messages. These can change the smartphone's state and maybe even, if the phone is set up for it, cause a so-called \textit{remote wipe}, so all stored messages and personal information are deleted. It is, however, not a simple task to prevent the phone from communicating via the telephone network without changing its state. Two techniques which can be used are:

\begin{itemize}
  \item To place the phone in a \textit{Faraday cage}. This is a technically secure, but rather expensive solution, which only professional investigators would normally have access to.
  \item To replace the phone's (U)SIM-card with a \textit{Cellular Network Isolation Card} (often abbreviated to \textit{CNIC}). This is a true copy of the (U)SIM-card, with the correct IMSI, MSISDN and so on, except for one thing: It does not contain the encryption key which would normally be shared with the network's Authentification Center. The phone can therefore not be attached to the network, but works normally in all other respects. To produce such a CNIC you need to have access to special equipment which can store information in a UICC smartcard.
\end{itemize}

Turning the phone off or putting it into \textit{flight mode} will disconnect it from all wireless networks (the telephone network, WiFi networks, Bluetooth etc.), but can give the investigators the problem that they need to know the PIN code for the SIM-card and the password or other form of user authentification in order to get the phone working again afterwards - for example, if further investigations turn out to be needed. Turning off the phone will of course also prevent taking a copy of the memory.

For many types of smartphone, there are tools which-with a somewhat bigger risk of changing the phone's state-can be used to investigate its content directly instead of a copy. A well-known example is \textit{Android Debug Bridge} (often known just as \textit{ADB}). This is a software tool that can run on an ordinary computer connected to an Android-based unit, such as a smartphone or tablet, via a USB cable. As the name indicates, ADB is really a tool for software developers to test and find faults in software for Android units. For that purpose the developer needs to be able to inspect the contents of the unit's memory, disks and so on, and this facility can also be used for forensic purposes. But, as with other tools for software testing, ADB also makes it possible to \textit{change} data in the unit under test, and thus to change the unit's state. The investigator must therefore be very careful only to look at things and not to change anything. Similar functionality is found in development environments (socalled \textit{IDE}s) for other OSs for mobile phones, such as \textit{Xcode} for iOS and \textit{Microsoft} \textit{Visual Studio} for Windows.

\section{A Short Interlude: Base64 Encoding}
Base64 encoding is a transformation of binary data-sequences of bits-to a sequence of characters from a 64-character alphabet. The steps in the transformation are as follows:

\begin{enumerate}
  \item Group the binary data into sequences of 3 bytes ($=24$ bits).
\end{enumerate}

\begin{itemize}
  \item If necessary, fill out to a multiple of 3 bytes by adding a suitable number of 0-bits as padding after the last byte.
\end{itemize}

\begin{enumerate}
  \setcounter{enumi}{1}
  \item Divide each sequence of 3 bytes up into 4 sequences of 6 bits.
  \item Encode each 6-bit sequence as a character, as specified in the encoding table. As there are 64 possible 6-bit sequences, the table will always contain 64 elements, which are customarily chosen from the printable characters. For HTTP authentication, the same table is used as for Base64 encoding of non-ASCII characters according to the MIME standards [39]. This is shown in Table 10.5.
  \item If 8 padding bits were added in Step 1, replace the last character from Step 3 by an equals sign (=). If 16 padding bits were added, replace the last two characters from Step 3 by equals signs.
\end{enumerate}

An example where "data" are just some text can be seen in Fig. 10.12. Each character in the text is represented by one byte (8 bits) in "ASCII code".

technological advances, modern disks with platters of around 6.25 cm ( 2.5 inches) can have capacities of 4 Tbyte or more.

Nowadays many so-called disks have no platters and no moving parts, but are purely electronic devices rather like computer memories. When there is no need for a motor, neither to rotate the disk nor to move the reading and writing heads, the disk can be lighter, completely silent and with lower power consumption. It is also very robust with respect to shocks and vibration, as there are no movable parts which can be shaken to pieces. All this is a big advantage in laptop computers and tablets. The primary example of this type of disk is the \emph{Solid State Drive}, often just called an \emph{SSD}. Even if the disk does not rotate, it is still conceptually divided up into tracks and sectors, so that from a programming point of view it is just a simple replacement for an ordinary rotating disk. And even though the actual SSD electronics take up very little room, the SSD is typically packed into a unit of the same size and with the same connecting plugs as a standard HDD , which it can physically replace.

When you need to read from or write to a particular place on a classical HDD, there is as a rule a considerable access time before reading or writing can begin. The disk needs to move the read/write heads to the desired track and also wait until the desired sector is under the heads. The rotation time is normally the largest contribution: on average it will be half the time for a complete rotation of the disk. For a disk which for example runs at 15000 rotations per minute, time for a complete rotation is 4 ms ., so the average rotation time will be 2 ms . In an SSD, there is nothing which needs to move, so the access time is a small fraction of a millisecond.

Though SSDs have all these advantages, they also have a number of disadvantages. Firstly, they are still much more expensive than rotating disks: an SSD with a given capacity for an ordinary PC, for example, costs in 2023 about 8-10 times as much as an HDD with the same capacity. Secondly, SSDs suffer from a kind of "electronic wear", so some of the small memory blocks in the SSD stop working after a certain number of write operations-typically between 5000 and 100000 , depending on the technology in use. The disk's control electronics attempts to counteract this by changing round which physical memory block gets written in, when the computer asks the disk to write a given block. The aim of this process, known as \emph{wear levelling}, is to ensure that all the physical blocks are used equally much.

Figure A. 4 shows schematically how wear levelling works: at the start, a given data block seen from the computer's side is written into the block with the same number in the SSD, as shown on the left in the figure. After a while, when a lot has been written in some of the blocks, for example blocks 1,5 and 19 , the disk electronics starts to use less-used blocks instead. So the block which the computer sees as block 1 now gets written to physical disk block 16, block 5 to physical block 13 and block 19 to physical block 21, as shown to the right in the figure. Paradoxically, even if the blocks in an SSD can be worn out, SSDs are difficult to delete completely. This is a potential security risk, if you need to delete confidential data.

Ways of dealing with damage can naturally be combined. Notice that some of them ( 1,2 and 3 ) are \textit{proactive} steps, which reduce the risk before the damage takes place, while others (4 and 5) are \textit{reactive} steps which are taken when the damage has in fact occurred.

\subsection{Risk Management}
\textit{Risk management} deals with all the activities which are related to evaluating and reducing risks. The part of it whose aim is to reduce risk to an acceptable level is often called \textit{risk mitigation}. There are five generally recognised strategies for this:

\section{Definition (Risk mitigation stategies)}
\begin{enumerate}
  \item \textbf{Risk avoidance:} Keep the target system away from given risks.\\
e.g.: Forbid risky behaviour such as use of WiFi.
  \item \textbf{Risk reduction:} Take proactive steps to prevent losses occurring or to reduce the extent of the loss.\\
e.g.: Make use of backups, encryption and so on.
  \item \textbf{Risk retention:} Allow a certain, agreed amount of "residual risk".\\
e.g.: Use reliable, but not redundant communication equipment.
  \item \textbf{Risk transfer:} Transfer the risk to others.\\
e.g.: Set up a contract for outsourcing.
  \item \textbf{Risk sharing:} Agree with other parties to deal with risks jointly.\\
e.g.: Agree on common facilities or mutual insurance.
\end{enumerate}

Irrespective of which strategy you choose, risk management must give a balance between three factors:

\begin{itemize}
  \item Security-how well is the IT system protected against unwanted events?
  \item Functionality-how well does the IT system perform its intended functions?
  \item Usability-how easy is it for users to make use of the system?
\end{itemize}

This last factor is unfortunately often forgotten by system designers, with the result that ordinary users spend a lot of time just trying to do simple tasks such as logging in to the system, transferring data or communicating with friends or colleagues, If security measures do not give a usable system, users will find ways to avoid them!

In order to develop a secure system, it is an advantage to use a systematic method, and over the years a number of systematic procedures for security analysis of IT systems have been developed. Some well-known examples are:

\subsection{Protection of Passwords}
Nowadays passwords are stored in the system in encrypted form (most often as a cryptographic hash of the password), so the unencrypted password cannot be found directly. But even with this way of doing things there are certain risks:

\begin{itemize}
  \item Easily available software, which only uses CPU power from an ordinary PC, can test an MD5 hash of a password against several hundred million candidate passwords per second. So a password with 8 randomly chosen letters from the English alphabet (A-Z) can be found via a brute-force attack in about 16 seconds. The organisation hashcat has published some benchmarks which show that if a computer with 8 modern GPUs (Nvidia Titan X) is used, then one can test several hundred billion candidates per second, so a password with 8 randomly chosen English letters can be found in a fraction of a second. On the other hand, a password with 8 randomly chosen characters from the character set \emph{ISO-latin-1} \emph{printable} will take 2 million seconds (about 23 days), while a password with 12 randomly chosen characters from that character set takes about 1 trillion seconds (around 32000 years). The time needed will in all cases be even longer if more complex hash functions, such as SHA-256 or bcrypt, are used.
  \item If the file with the encrypted passwords is available, it is easy to try to encrypt all the words in a dictionary, to see whether one of them matches. On the Internet you can find large collections of potential passwords encrypted using various hash functions. Moreover, these collections include not only words which can be found in an ordinary dictionary, but also commonly used modifications of ordinary words (such as replacing the letter 'o' with the digit ' 0 ', letter ' B ' with digit '3' or the like) and passwords found through previous password cracking attempts. Given such a collection, the attacker does not even need to use time for calculating the hash values-simply searching in the collection to find a match for the stored hash value will lead directly to the password in plaintext.
  \item If several users use the same password, the hash values stored in the file will be identical.
\end{itemize}

A problem with FDE is that it requires special tricks to start the system. It is obvious that at least some parts of the OS have to be decrypted before the OS can be started. But where should the decryption functions and keys be stored? A simple solution would be to let a small area on the disk, containing decryption software and keys, remain unencrypted, but this is plainly not a secure way of solving the problem. A more secure approach is to use \textit{pre-boot authentication}, a technique where a specially hardened mini-OS, whose integrity can easily be checked on the basis of its cryptographic checksum, is used to start the main OS. The mini-OS will only start the main OS if it receives a particular ``external key'' which acts as a proof of the user's identity. More or less all the user authentication methods which were discussed at the start of this chapter can in principle be used: a password, a biometric measurement, a smartcard (or even just a flash drive) containing a PIN code or other unique form of identification.

The use of transparent encryption presupposes that the encryption system has constant access to the necessary encryption and decryption keys. But the keys are themselves very sensitive pieces of information which must be protected. This can be done by software which maintains a \textit{keystore}, as in many Windows-based systems, or a \textit{keyring}, as in many Unix-based systems. The keystore/keyring is itself encrypted, typically with a key which is specific for the individual user.

Alternatively, the keys can be stored in a hardware unit, either in the form of a smartcard, which the user if necessary can carry round, or in a \textit{Trusted Platform Module (TPM)}, which is typically built in to the computer itself. A TPM is a unit, constructed in accordance with International Standard \textit{ISO/IEC 11889:2009}, which can generate new keys, encrypt and decrypt data and calculate cryptographic checksums. TPMs are used for ensuring the integrity of IT systems' configuration, in order to prevent unauthorised replacement of hardware or software components, and are also frequently used in control units for disks with FDE. When smartcards or TPMs are used for encryption of data, it is typically possible to keep the keys inside the hardware unit, so they are never—not even temporarily—stored in the computer's memory, where a crafty attacker could get hold of them.

When the keys are stored and fetched by using software, it is possible for a technically knowledgeable attacker to find the keys, since typical software-based encryption systems save the keys in characteristic places in the computer's memory. And even if they do not save the main key for more than a moment, software solutions which use round-based encryption algoritms, such as \textit{AES} or \textit{3DES}, often store the \textit{round keys} in order to save time. From these round keys it is often possible to work back to the value of the main key.

This is especially thought to be a problem if an attacker finds or steals a laptop PC or tablet which is running or in the \textit{standby state}, as it can then be woken up without going through the entire startup procedure. The machine can be attacked by a so-called \textit{cold boot} attack, where the machine is restarted from a removable disk containing a simple OS, which is used to copy the machine's memory into a file. Even if the machine is turned off during the restart procedure, the content of the memory will survive for a few seconds — long enough to copy it for further investigation. The attack does not work if the machine is completely turned off or in the \textit{hibernate} state, as it is then necessary to go through the normal startup procedure where the contents of the memory are initialised and any keys therefore disappear.

\textbf{Example 1:} Suppose Alice discovers that Bob uses the same modulus. Since she knows her own two exponents ($p_{A}, s_{A}$), she can efficiently factorise $n$ and find $q$ and $r$. Once she knows these, and also knows Bob's public exponent, $p_{B}$, she can easily derive Bob's private exponent, $s_{B}$, and Bob's security is completely compromised.

\textbf{Example 2:} If Mallet is an attacker who does not know any of the private exponents, she can use another approach. Suppose that Alice and Bob with public exponents respectively $p_{A}$ and $p_{B}$ encrypt $d$ to obtain the ciphertexts $e_{A}$ and $e_{B}$:

\[
\begin{aligned}
& e_{A}=d^{p_{A}} \bmod n \\
& e_{B}=d^{p_{B}} \bmod n
\end{aligned}
\]

Then, if $\operatorname{gcd}\left(p_{A}, p_{B}\right)=1$ (in other words, $p_{A}$ and $p_{B}$ have no common factors, which is usually the case), Mallet can make use of Euclid's Extended Algorithm (see Sect. B. 4 in App. B) to find integers $u$ and $v$ such that: $u \times p_{A}+v \times p_{B}=1$. She can then recover the plaintext, $d$, by evaluating $e_{A}{ }^{u} \times e_{B}{ }^{v}$, without needing to find any of the users' private exponents, $s_{A}$ and $s_{B}$, at all. More details of the mathematics behind this attack can be found in Sect. B. 7 in Appendix B.

As RSA is a so-called \textit{deterministic} encryption algorithm, an encryption of the same plaintext with the same key will always give the same ciphertext. This makes it possible to attack RSA by using a \textit{chosen plaintext attack}-you choose a number of likely plaintexts and produce the corresponding ciphertexts to see whether they match a piece of ciphertext which you have got hold of. To avoid this form of attack, it is standard practice to pad out the plaintext with a number of randomly chosen \textit{padding bits} before encrypting it. Standards such as \textit{PKCS\#1} [54] describe secure ways to produce these \textit{padding bits}, so repeated encryptions of the same plaintext will be very unlikely to produce the same ciphertext. Padding with randomly chosen bit sequences will also prevent attacks which exploit the use of small public exponents.

You should also notice that the RSA cryptosystem, just like the stream ciphers discussed in Sect. 4.3.5, is \textit{malleable}. That is to say, an attacker who sees a ciphertext without knowing the corresponding plaintext can form a valid ciphertext for a completely different plaintext. The ciphertext for the original message $m$ and key $p$ is evaluated as $\mathcal{E}(m, p)=m^{p} \bmod n$. An attacker can form the ciphertext for $m \times t$ for any value $t$ by evaluating $\mathcal{E}(m, p) \times t^{p} \bmod n$, which is equal to $(m \times t)^{p} \bmod n=\mathcal{E}(m \times t, p)$. This implies that you need to take suitable steps to ensure the message's \textit{integrity} in order to prevent this type of manipulation. This topic is discussed in the next chapter.

\subsection{IEEE 802.11 Modes of Operation}
A wireless network which is built up in accordance with the 802.11 standard can operate in two different \textit{modes}, known as \textit{Infrastructure Mode} and \textit{Ad hoc Mode}.

Infrastructure Mode, illustrated in Fig. 6.17, is the mode which most resembles the modes of operation used in other types of radio-based network:

\begin{itemize}
  \item There is a wireless network card in each station ("STA").
  \item STAs can only communicate with one another via an \textit{Access Point (AP)}.
  \item A group of STAs attached to a given AP make up a \textit{Basic Service Set (BSS)}.
  \item Multiple APs (= multiple BSSs) are connected via a cable-based infrastructure to form an \textit{Extended Service Set (ESS)}.
  \item An ESS is identified by a \textit{Service Set IDentifier (SSID)}, which is typically a name in ordinary text. When you turn on a WiFi device to connect to a WiFi network, you use the SSID to select which network to connect to.
\end{itemize}

In Ad hoc Mode, illustrated in Fig. 6.18, there is still a wireless network card in every station but no APs, so the individual stations make up a BSS in which they can communicate directly with one another. This can be a security risk, as each participant has to rely on all the others being well-behaved, as there is no AP between them to perform any sort of control.

\section{Definition (GDPR terms (Source: [32]))}
\begin{itemize}
  \item \textbf{Personal data:} Any information relating to an identified or identifiable natural person (a \textit{data subject})
  \item \textbf{Processing:} Any operation or set of operations performed on personal data, whether or not by automatic means.
  \item \textbf{Controller:} The natural or legal person, public authority, agency or other body, which determines the purposes and means of the processing of personal data.
  \item \textbf{Processor:} A natural or legal person, public authority, agency or other body which performs the processing on behalf of the controller.
  \item \textbf{Recipient:} A natural or legal person, public authority, agency or other body, to which the personal data are disclosed. (With the exception of authorities who receive such data in an enquiry defined by law.)
  \item \textbf{Consent:} A freely given, specific, informed and unambiguous indication, by which the data subject, in a clear affirmative action, signifies agreement to the processing of personal data related to him or her.
  \item \textbf{Personal data breach:} A breach of security leading to the accidental or unlawful destruction, loss, alteration, unauthorised disclosure of, or access to, personal data which are transmitted, stored or otherwise processed.
  \item \textbf{Pseudonymisation:} Processing of personal data in such a way that they cannot be attributed to a specific data subject without using additional information. Such information must be kept separately and under suitable safeguards.
  \item \textbf{Profiling:} Automatic processing of personal data to evaluate certain personal aspects of a natural person, such as the person's performance at work, economic situation, health, preferences, interests, behaviour etc.
\end{itemize}

\subsection{Investigation of Security Incidents}
Investigation of security incidents is a special discipline, which in many ways resembles a police investigation in criminal cases: You have a suspicion of a possible crime and try to collect evidence which can reveal what has happened and (if possible) who lies behind it. This discipline is generally known as \emph{Computer Forensics}, by analogy with other forms of collection of criminal evidence and finding chains of causes and consequences.

Incidents such as break-ins, theft, vandalism and natural disasters have very little to do with cybersecurity and they are investigated in the usual way. But incidents such as loss of availability, hacker attacks, virus attacks or unwanted disclosure, loss or modification of data as a rule require the computers which have been affected to be investigated. As it is important not to lose important evidence, this investigation must be carried out according to some special rules---the material may have to be used in a subsequent court case and must therefore be collected, analysed and stored with great care. A typical set of principles (from the British police) for ``good practice'' can be seen in [100].

The investigators need a true picture of:

\begin{enumerate}
  \item The affected system's \emph{state}---that is to say the content of all parts of the computer where data can be stored: the memory, disks, other external media, the CPU registers etc.
  \item If possible, some of the system's recent \emph{history}; this normally comes from \emph{log files}, where significant events are noted down in their order of occurrence.
\end{enumerate}

\subsection{The BlottoX worm}
A new type of malware, known as BlottoX, is a worm which attacks computers running Windows operating systems. It propagates itself by exploiting the Remote Desktop Protocol (RDP). It may download further malicious software, which acts as a backdoor to the infected computer.

When the worm arrives at an uninfected computer and is executed, it first copies itself to the file cache.txt in the Windows folder which is used for storing offline web pages. It then copies the standard file sens.dll in Windows' system folder to a new file, Sens32.dll, in the same folder and stores a copy of itself in sens.dll.

BlottoX then searches to find DNS records for three domains which the attackers themselves have registered:

\begin{verbatim}
ms.jifr.co.be
ms.jifr.co.cc
ss.jifr.net
\end{verbatim}

Some of these records can be DNS TXT records that contain information about backdoors which the worm can download. All such backdoors are fetched by using FTP from the URI \href{http://errormail.tonzobark.ru/160.rar}{errormail.tonzobark.ru/160.rar}. The worm will then inject itself into the generic Windows service svchost.exe, so it will be executed if a process based on this service is started. It then deletes the file which contains the original copy of the worm code.

Next, BlottoX attempts to terminate the execution of all processes which contain text strings (such as avguard, FortiScand, mcshield, SpySweeper etc.), which apparently identify them as being security products such as antivirus or antispyware programs.

Finally the worm tries to propagate itself to other computers in the local network by using RDP. It opens TCP connections to the standard port 3389 on each of these computers and tries a large number of simple userid/password combinations—for example, with userids such as administrator, admin, test, user and guest, and passwords such as 1, 1234, 111111, password, \%u\%, 1q2w3e, secret and other combinations which are easy to guess. If it succeeds in setting up an RDP connection to another computer, the worm transfers itself to that computer.

Imagine you are the person responsible for cybersecurity in the company Target Llc. The company has installed a behavioural HIDS based on anomaly detection in each computer in its network. Would you expect that this IDS could detect some (or all?) of the activities which are set going by the BlottoX worm? Explain your answer—for example by giving conditions for being able to detect the individual activities or arguments for why it would not be possible.

\subsection{Establishing an Identity}
In order for some party, say Alice, to obtain any sort of documentation for identity, such as a certificate, it is obviously essential that Alice is able to produce suitable evidence which demonstrates that she really is who she claims to be. How easy this is to do depends on two main factors:

\begin{enumerate}
  \item Exactly what sort of entity Alice really is. For example, is Alice actually a human being or just an IT system, such as a server.
  \item The degree of confidence which we want to have in the claimed identity.
\end{enumerate}

Publicly accessible IT systems in the Internet are very easy to deal with, as each such entity has a globally unique \emph{Internet name} which has been registered in the Internet's \emph{Domain Name System}, which we look at in more detail in Chap. 6. This registration process may be assumed to be trustworthy. If for example we then need an X. 500 name for use in an X 509 v 3 certificate, we can just use the Internet name as one of the attributes (typically the Common Name (CN) attribute) to create a unique X. 500 name for use in the certificate.

The other common simple case is when we want to have documentation for the identity of a client such as a web browser or e-mail client. In this case, too, it is easy to find a globally unique name which can be used in the certificate-namely, the name of the user's e-mail account: \href{mailto:fred.snooks@nowhere.eu}{fred.snooks@nowhere.eu} or whatever. It is easy for a supplier of credentials for this purpose to check that this account exists by simply sending it an e-mail with instructions on how to intall the credentials themselves. Despite the risk of spoofing, this is normally enough to provide at least a limited degree of confidence in the correctness of the identity.

Part of the investigator's task can therefore be to find out which disks have actually been \textit{mounted}, so that they have been accessible from the computer to be investigated. A table in the operating system contains information about the current status. Most modern operating systems also record in a log file when disks are mounted and unmounted. So the investigator can if necessary see whether further disks have been in use in the period just before the incident was detected.

It is important to realise that it is not enough just to copy the files from the disk one by one to a new non-volatile medium such as an external disk or USB key. This is due to two phenomena:

\begin{enumerate}
  \item Except in specially secured operating systems, deletion of a file will \textit{not} result in deletion of the file's data content, but only that the file will be marked as deleted in the file catalog. The areas on the disk where the file's contents are stored are first overwritten when they need to be re-used for new files. Data from the deleted files may contain information which is useful for the investigation. But as the files have been deleted, they will not be included in a file-by-file copy.
  \item There may also be areas on the disk which do not contain ordinary files, but contain data for administrative purposes, such as so-called \textit{Master Boot Records} for use during system startup. These may also have been altered as part of an attack.
\end{enumerate}

Instead of a file-by-file copy, it is therefore necessary to create a so-called \textit{bit-by-bit} \textit{copy} of the whole disk.

This task is as a rule very easy in systems based on a \textit{virtual machine (VM)}, since in most VM systems it is possible to take a \textit{snapshot} of the machine's state. In other system types you need to copy from a physical disk to another medium. \subsection{More Secure Key Agreements}
What is missing in order to prevent this type of active attack on the Diffie-Hellman protocol is information which identifies the sender of a message (in other words: authentication), and information which ensures integrity.

The security is improved if an \emph{electronic signature} is added to Diffie-Hellman messages as a proof of their origin. A well-known example of an improved protocol is the so-called \emph{station-to-station protocol} shown in Fig. 5.15. As in the original Diffie-Hellman protocol, the agreed key $K$ is $(\alpha^{x_{A} \cdot x_{B}} \bmod q)$. With these additions to the Diffie-Hellman protocol, attackers cannot replace $\alpha^{x_{A}}$ by $\alpha^{x'_{A}}$ or $\alpha^{x_{B}}$ by $\alpha^{x'_{B}}$ without this being detected, as they cannot forge the signatures.

Message 1\quad $A \rightarrow B$: $\alpha^{x_{A}} \bmod q$

Message 2\quad $B \rightarrow A$: $(\alpha^{x_{B}} \bmod q, \mathcal{E}(S_{B}(\alpha^{x_{B}}, \alpha^{x_{A}}), K))$

Message 3\quad $A \rightarrow B$: $\mathcal{E}(S_{A}(\alpha^{x_{B}}, \alpha^{x_{A}}), K)$

\subsection{Certificates}
Certificates are digital documents which guarantee which public key belongs to a given subject. They are an essential ingredient in so-called \emph{Public Key Infrastructure} (\emph{PKI}) systems, where they are used to determine identity. They are used in all contexts where it is necessary to know a subject’s public key—for example, when verifying electronic signatures and for authentication. The certificates in a PKI system are issued by a \emph{Certificate Authority (CA)}, which the owner and potential recipients of the certificate need to trust.

The completely essential components in a certificate are, as we have seen, the owner’s identity and public key, signed with the issuer’s electronic signature, but in practice most certificates contain additional information. The commonest structure today is for so-called \emph{X.509v3 certificates} — that is to say, they follow version 3 of the ITU-T standard X.509. This structure is shown in Fig. 5.16.

The signature algorithm is described by specifying which encryption algorithm and (if required) hash function is used for calculating the signature, e.g. PKCS $\# 1$ SHA-1 with \emph{RSA} encryption. \subsection{Bypassing Access Control: Rootkits}
As ordinary operating systems give extensive privileges to a subject which has a status as administrator (or "root"), it is a natural aim for an attacker to try to achieve this status. This phenomenon is known as \emph{privilege escalation}. Typically this is achieved by exploiting a software vulnerability such as one of those described in Chap. 10, or by misusing a service which has been configured to run with high privileges, such as a web browser or database server running with the privileges of the root user.

An alternative approach is to use a type of malware known as a \emph{rootkit}. The name "rootkit" arose because the first generation of these used privilege escalation in order to achieve root privileges, and then used cloaking techniques to hide their presence in the victim computer. Modern rootkits have hiding their malicious payload as their primary objective. This enables the attacker to remain undetected in its victim for a long period, during which it can for example monitor user activity, collect up passwords or other credentials, or act as part of a botnet to send out spam mail or perform DDoS attacks.

Well-constructed rootkits are really good at hiding their presence, so they can sit in a computer for a very long time without being detected. Typically they will at the very least take steps to modify system programs for listing files and processes, so that the rootkit's files and processes do not appear in the lists. They may also turn off the victim's event logging system, if there is one, so as to prevent evidence of the attack being recorded. Some also turn off the antivirus system, so as to avoid detection of their malicious payload and its effcts.

Originally, rootkits were something you only saw in Unix-based operating systems. More recently, however, rootkits for several variants of Windows, for hypervisors for virtual machines, for BIOS and other firmware have turned up. The infamous \emph{Stuxnet} worm, which was used to attack industrial software, even contained a rootkit for a PLC, which is a very primitive form of computer.

Rootkits can be designed to run in different CPU modes, and therefore with different possibilities for exploiting the machine's instructions. The simplest and least privileged are \emph{user mode rootkits}, which run with the CPU in user mode

\subsection{LDAP Searches}
LDAP is a multifunctional client-server protocol, which makes it possible to insert, modify, delete and search for objects in an LDAP database. Here we focus solely on searching, as it is this function which in practice is most exposed to attacks. To search in the database, the client typically constructs a URI which identifies an LDAP server and specifies where in the DIT hierarchy the search is to take place, and what is to be searched for. The general form of the URI is:
\textit{ldap://host:port/dn?attributes?scope?filter?extensions}

The various components of the URI are as follows:
host An Internet name or IP address for the server.
port The number of the port to be used on the server.
dn A DN which identifies the \textit{base}-the object in the hierarchy, where the search is to start.
attributes A comma-separated list of attributes, whose values are to be sent back to the client.
scope The extent of the search in relation to the base. Possible values (see Fig. 10.10) are: \textit{base} the search only includes the base. \textit{one} the search includes all successors of the base which lie one level below the base in the hierarchy. \textit{sub} the search includes the base and all its successors in the hierarchy.
filter A set of rules for selection of objects which are to be considered within the given \textit{scope}.
extensions A comma-separated list of LDAP extensions which are to be used.

Most of these components can be left out. If \textit{host} is omitted, the client must be configured to use a particular server. If \textit{port} is omitted, TCP port 389 (or, if LDAPS is used, port 636) is used. If \textit{dn} is omitted, the empty DN, "", is used, so the search starts at the top of the hierarchy. If \textit{attributes} is omitted, all attributes are sent to the client. If \textit{scope} is omitted, base is used. If \textit{filter} is omitted, (objectClass=*) is used, so all types of object within the chosen scope are searched. If extensions is omitted, no extensions are selected.

SHA-3 is based on a so-called \textit{sponge construction}, where the basic step to incorporate a block of the message into the final result is illustrated in Fig. 5.4. The state is divided into two parts, known as R (the \textit{rate}: $r$ bits) and C (the \textit{capacity}: $c$ bits). Both R and C are initialised to 0. In each step, an input block is mixed with the R part of the current state using an XOR function, and then the function $f$ is applied to both parts of the state to produce a \textit{random permutation} of the $(r+c)$ bits in the state. After the last block of input has been dealt with, the actual $n$-bit hash value is derived from the $r$ bits in the R part of the final state.

With the sponge construction, the security strength against preimage attacks is $n$ bits, and the strength against collision attacks is $n/2$ bits as usual. The strength against length extension attacks depends on the size of the capacity, $c$ bits, which in the final version of the standard is equal to $2n$. The reason that SHA-3 is so resistant to length extension is that the content of C is never output, so it is not possible for an external attacker to find the entire final state-a pre-requisite for performing the attack in a simple way.

MD5 is no longer considered secure: Its digest length is too small, and its security strength against collisions is much less than 64, so it is by no means collision-free. In 2016, a group from Google succeeded in finding some collisions for SHA-1. It has been known for some time that there was a theoretical possibility of collisions, as its effective security strength is around 63 bits. $2^{63}$ is still a large number (about 9 billion billion), but the team from Google managed to create two different PDF documents with the same SHA-1 hash value. This was a big effort: the calculation took a total of \textit{6610 years} of CPU time. Nevertheless, SHA-2 or SHA-3 are recommended for use from now on.

\section{The Chinese Remainder Theorem}
The Chinese remainder theorem is yet another antique discovery, which comes from the Chinese mathematician Sun-Tsu, who worked around 100 AD:

\section{Theorem (Chinese Remainder Theorem)}
\emph{Given a set of $k$ equivalences using modular arithmetic:}
$$
x \equiv a_{1} \;\left(\bmod m_{1}\right), \quad x \equiv a_{2} \;\left(\bmod m_{2}\right), \ldots, \quad x \equiv a_{k} \;\left(\bmod m_{k}\right)
$$
\emph{then there is a unique solution for $x\left(\bmod m_{1} \times m_{2} \ldots \times m_{k}\right)$, if the individual moduli $\left(m_{1}, m_{2}, \ldots, m_{k}\right)$ are mutual primes—that is to say, that for each pair of moduli, $m_{i}$ and $m_{j}$ (where $i \neq j$), then $\operatorname{gcd}\left(m_{i}, m_{j}\right)=1$.}

\textbf{An example:} Find a solution for $x$, given that:
$$
x \equiv 4 \;(\bmod 5), \quad x \equiv 5 \;(\bmod 11)
$$

A simple way of solving the problem when the numbers are small is to list the first few integers which are congruent to 5, when we use modulo 11 arithmetic. They are:

$$
5, 16, 27, 38, 49, 60, 71, \ldots
$$

If we work modulo 5, these numbers have the values $0,1,2,3,4,0,1, \ldots$ respectively. As we want to find the number which has the value $4 \;(\bmod 5)$, the solution must be $x=49 \;(\bmod 5 \times 11)$.

Sam, who knows all the secret keys, now reads the authenticator and constructs a new one, which is still encrypted with $SK_{BS}$, but now also contains the new secret key, $SK_{AB}$, which Alice and Bob will share in their further communication:

$$
\mathcal{E}\big((A, N_{B}, SK_{AB}), SK_{BS}\big)
$$

This is sent in Message 4 from Sam to Alice tgether with Bob's identifier, Alice's nonce and the new key. Message 4 is encrypted with the secret key which Alice shares with Sam, so the new secret cannot be revealed to anyone other than Alice.

Alice can now check that the reply from Sam in Message 4 contains precisely the nonce that Alice herself chose, and that no attackers have changed the identification of the party, Bob, whom Alice would like to communicate with. This might have happened if an attacker had modified Message 3 or replaced it with an old ``Message 3'' from a previous exchange. If everything seems to be OK, Alice accepts $SK_{AB}$ as the right key to use for communication with Bob, and sends Bob (in Message 5) the extended authenticator, which Alice has just received from Sam. As it is encrypted with $SK_{BS}$, Bob can decrypt it, get hold of the new secret key and check that the nonce is Bob's own, $N_{B}$. This shows that the message is not a replay of an old ``Message 5''. Bob can now conclude that the trustworthy Sam can vouch for Alice being the other party.

The last two messages are needed to convince Alice and Bob that the other actually exists and has got hold of the key $SK_{AB}$. In Message 6, Bob uses the new key to send a new nonce to Alice, who modifies it in some agreed manner (here just indicated by subtracting 1 from the value of the nonce) to protect against a replay performed by an attacker. She then sends the modified value, encrypted with the new key, to Bob. Alice and Bob are now able to communicate confidentially with one another-and subsequently also to authenticate themselves to one another by using the new key.

d) \textbf{Provide subscriber data} for telecomms services which the person offers. Subscriber data involves information, such as the subscriber's name, address, telephone number, billing information, information on installed communications equipment etc., which is available on the basis of a service agreement or similar.

In addition, the authorities must be able to \textit{search and possibly seize} computers and storage media for computers, take copies of computer data, maintain the integrity of these computer data and if necessary make computer data inaccessible.

Finally, the authorities must be able to collect in \textit{real time}, to the extent this is technically possible, certain data with relation to specific communications within the authority's territory. This covers:
a) \textbf{Collection of traffic data}, defined as above.
b) \textbf{Collection of content data}, i.e. the content of the messages which are transmitted.

Collection of such data can be performed by the authorities themselves, or they can oblige a service provider to perform the task for them.

Especially this part of the convention is somewhat controversial, as collection of data can be seen as making inroads into citizens' private lives, and possibly even as a threat to freedom of expression. Moreover, it makes life difficult for service providers, who have to install equipment for rapid collection and large-scale storage of data. In many countries, the laws on the administration of justice allow the authorities to require the data to be kept for up to 90 days. So if the surveillance in fact lasts longer than 90 days, the telecomms operator risks having to store 90 days' traffic. In a modern, fast telecommunications network this will correspond to a very large volume of data.

On the other hand, the convention makes clear that the powers which the authorities are granted via Section 2 of the convention's Chapter II must respect the individual country's existing rules for the protection of human rights and liberties, including \textit{"rights arising pursuant to obligations it has undertaken under the 1950 Council of Europe Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms, the 1966 United Nations International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights, and other applicable international human rights instruments"}. Typically, this form of surveillance requires permission from a court of justice.

\subsection{Jurisdiction}
It is in the nature of things that cybercrime can be a cross-border activity, and therefore it is important to define who it is that has \textit{jurisdiction}-the right to make legal decisions-over the crimes listed in the convention. The principal rule is that a state has jurisdiction over crimes committed in its territory. Furthermore, a country can decide that its jurisdiction must also cover crimes committed:

\begin{itemize}
  \item on board a ship, which sails under the flag of that country, or
  \item on board a plane, which is registered in accordance with the laws of that country, or
  \item by a citizen of that country, if the crime is punishable where it was committed, or if the crime was committed outside the territorial jurisdiction of any state.
\end{itemize}

Experience shows that it is especially with respect to giving priorities to the assets that the different groups may disagree. At a university or other knowledgebased enterprise, for example, it is a not unusual to find that:

\begin{itemize}
  \item The management focus on things which they must use in the daily administration, and on things which affect the organisation's external image. For example:
  \item that important e-mails from the top management are always available,
  \item that confidential information-either internally generated or coming from outside-is to be kept confidential.
  \item The IT staff focus on things which experience shows lead to operational disturbances and on functions such as backup and physical breakdown of technical assets.
  \item Ordinary employees focus on their knowledge production and on material which they need for meetings, discussions and other forms of dissemination, all of which must be available come what may.
\end{itemize}

To proceed from there, the management therefore appoint an experienced \textit{analysis group}, who can get these different priorities and security targets to hang together and then move on to the threat analysis.

You should note that in Phase 1 it is only the assets which are prioritisednaturally in relation to their significance for the organisation's activities. Starting from a possibly very long list of assets, the analysis group tries to identify the socalled \textit{critical assets}, without which the organisation would not be able to perform its tasks.

In Phase 2, an analysis is carried out of the extent to which the organisation's infrastructure (especially its most important components) contains vulnerabilities which can be exploited for threats to the critical assets. The costs of protecting the assets are not considered before Phase 3, and then it is a question of how much one is willing to pay in order to reduce the risk of damage to an acceptable level.

When the analysis group has reached agreement on which assets are critical, they try to identify the threats which could affect these assets. Their starting point will typically be the concerns and fault scenarios which were indicated by the three key groups. Further inspiration can, if necessary, be found by using models such as \textit{STRIDE}, in which one considers what can go wrong within 6 main areas:

\begin{enumerate}
  \item \textbf{S}poofing: Faking identity
  \item \textbf{T}ampering: Unauthorised modification of data
  \item \textbf{R}epudiation: Denial of having performed an action
  \item \textbf{I}nformation disclosure: Loss of confidentiality
  \item \textbf{D}enial of service (DoS): Loss of availability
  \item \textbf{E}levation of privilege: Gaining more rights
\end{enumerate}

Regardless of how you find the potential threats, they then have to be described in more detail. This is done in OCTAVE by creating \textit{threat profiles} for each threat.

\subsection{OCTAVE Threat Profiles}
Each threat which is identified is described by a threat profile which characterises it in relation to five standard properties:

Asset: The \textit{IT asset} which is threatened.\\
Actor: Who or what causes a breach of the (CIA) security targets for the asset? Is the actor within the organisation or outside it?\\[0pt]
[Motive:] Is the actor's action performed deliberately or by accident?\\[0pt]
[Access:] How did the actor access the asset? By being physically present or by technical means such as using a network?\\
Outcome: What happens to the asset? Is it disclosure, modification, destruction/loss or interruption?

Motive and Access are not relevant for all types of threat and can then be left out.

Note that the "asset" in a threat scenario must be the \textit{IT asset} which is exposed to the threat. For example; a collection of data, some software, some hardware, or a complete IT system made up of a combination of such elements.

\subsection{OCTAVE Threat Classes}
In OCTAVE, threats are divided up into four standard classes, depending on the origin of the threat, as described in Definition 3.2

\section{Definition (OCTAVE Threat Classes:)}
\begin{enumerate}
  \item The threat comes from a human actor who accesses the asset by technical means such as via a network.
  \item The threat comes from a human actor who has physical access to the asset.
  \item System problems, i.e. problems with the organisation's IT systems. \textit{E.g. Hardware defects, software defects, system crashes, malicious code, etc.}
  \item Other problems, i.e. situations outside the organisation's control. \textit{E.g. Natural disasters, power failures, telecomms failures, failures in third-party systems, etc.}
\end{enumerate}

There are standard profile templates for threats which fall into each of these classes. These are normally drawn in the form of \textit{threat trees}, whose root identifies the critical asset which is exposed to the threat, and whose leaves show the outcome. The path from the root of the tree to the leaf shows the actor and motive for the threat to the relevant critical asset, as can be seen in the examples in Figs. 3.6, 3.7 and 3.8.

\section{The Operating System}
The Operating System forms the basis on which applications can be built up: it hides the details of the operation of the hardware and offers a uniform interface-a so-called \textit{Application Program Interface}, often called an \textit{API} for short-which the actual applications can match. An OS is therefore a fundamental software component in more or less all modern computers. The only common exceptions are the small embedded computers which can be found in pieces of apparatus, household equipment and the like. It is easy to see the advantages of having such a uniform interface to applications, if you think that OSs such as Windows, Linux and Android have to be able to run on many different hardware platforms. It would be unbearable, if the developers had to adapt all their application programs individually to each platform.

There are a very large number of different operating systems - Wikipedia, for example, has a list of several hundred which have been in use at one time or another since the 1960s [99]. These include OSs designed for general purpose use and OSs for systems with special properties such as the ability to handle events with strict timing requirements, mobility, or a high level of security, or which are designed for specific computer architectures.

In spite of this variety, there are a number of features which appear in most of them:

\begin{itemize}
  \item \textbf{Drivers}, which handle the individual physical hardware units attached to the system, so the users can avoid having to know the units' design and internal workings.
  \item \textbf{Multiprogramming}, which makes it possible for several programs to run simultaneously on the same hardware. This leads to a number of requirements for the operating system, which must offer:
  \begin{itemize}
    \item Protection: User $A$'s program and data must not be able to disturb the execution of user $B$'s program.
    \item Controlled access to the computer's resources, such as:
    \begin{itemize}
      \item The CPU
      \item The storage units
      \item Input- and output units
      \item Networks
    \end{itemize}
    \item Sharable programs, such as libraries of useful functions.
    \item Sharable data
    \item File systems, which make it possible to organise programs and data into independent, named files, which are collected up in a hierarchy of named folders. A file system's software functions deal with keeping track of where on the disk there is unused space in which things can be stored, and in general free the user from having to deal directly with the computer's disks.
    \item User control, so only authorised users can use the computer-and only for what they are authorised to do.
    \item Handling the user interface, so the users can interact with the computer in a (more or less) convenient manner.
    \item Logging of important events in the computer. Typically a number of files are used to store information about user activity, updates, errors and other irregularities.
  \end{itemize}
\end{itemize}

The Response value is evaluated in three steps which depend on which qop was chosen. In the most common version, where qop=auth, the steps are:

\begin{enumerate}

If \textit{qop} is not specified in the Challenge, the client must not supply a cnonce or nc, and nc:cnonce:qop is omitted from this last calculation, so the Response value is reduced to \textit{H} (HA1:nonce:HA2), as in the original version of the protocol described in RFC2069.

It turns out that when we do arithmetic modulo $n$, then an integer only has an inverse if it is mutually prime with $n$, i.e. it has no common factors with $n$. If $n$ itself is a prime number (as 5 and 7 are), there will therefore always be ( $n-1$ ) integers which have an inverse. If $n$ is the product of two prime numbers, $q$ and $r$ (as 6 is), there will be ( $q-1) \times(r-1)$ integers which have an inverse. The number of integers with inverses when we do arithmetic modulo $n$ is often written $\phi(n)$. The function $\phi$ (pronounced "fy") is known as Euler's totient function. These results have significance for some of the asymmetric cryptosystems which we present below.

The modulo operation itself does not have an inverse function: Even if you know that the value of $a$ mod 5 is 1 , you cannot unambiguously calculate $a$ 's value. Therefore it is often used in the construction of trapdoor functions, such as:

\begin{itemize}
  \item Modular Exponentiation: $e=d^{p}$ mod $n$ $\mathcal{E}^{-1}$ : Calculate the integer $p$ 'th root of $e$ modulo $n$. That is to say, the integer which, when $p$ copies of it are multiplied together modulo $n$, gives $e$.
  \item Modular Squaring: $e=d^{2} \bmod n$ $\mathcal{E}^{-1}$ : Calculate the integer square root of $e$ modulo $n$. That is to say, the integer which, when multiplied by itself modulo $n$, gives $e$.
  \item Modul\ae r Exponentiation: $e=b^{d}$ mod $n$ $\mathcal{E}^{-1}$ : Calculate the discrete logarithm to the base $b$ of $e$ modulo $n$. That is to say, the integer which indicates how many copies of $b$ must be multiplied together modulo $n$ to give $e$.
\end{itemize}
